title: Effects of environmental sound quality on soundscape preference in a public urban space
research_question: How does environmental sound quality influence visitors' soundscape perceptions, preferences, and behavior in a public urban space?

participants.description: Visitors of Sha Tin Park, Hong Kong. 71.3% female, 28.7% male. 49.3% visited every day, 35.3% 3-4 times per week. 53.3% stayed 30-60 mins. Most common aims: playing with children (32%), sports (24.7%), rest (14.6%). Excluded individuals with self-reported hearing problems.
participants.recruitment: Self-administered questionnaires were distributed to visitors in five locations at Sha Tin Park.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Five distinct locations within Sha Tin Park, Hong Kong: G1 (North garden), P1 (North garden children playground), P2 (South garden children playground), G2 (South garden), and G3 (South garden entrance). Objective acoustic measurements were taken at these locations.

The acoustic environment of the five park locations, characterized by various objective acoustic and psychoacoustic metrics (e.g., Lzeq, LAeq, Neq, Seq, Lzmax, LAmax, Nmax, LA10, LA50, LA90, LA10-LA90).

measures.instrument: Semantic differential scale (1-5, Not to be preferred-To be preferred) for 11 elements (bird, water, wind, insect, human activity, music, pet, chatting, children playing, traffic, construction sounds)

measures.construct: Overall preference for a good soundscape

mechanisms: The psychoacoustic metric Sharpness (S) is sensitive to the spectral content of sounds, indicating that the perception of sound variation is affected more by spectral content than energy content.
Human voice, as a low-frequency sound source, contributes to higher maximum sound levels (LAmax) and lower Sharpness (S) in playground environments.

Maximum noise levels (LAmax, Nmax) and the range of noise levels (LA10 - LA90) are more important than time-equivalent noise levels (LAeq) in predicting visitors' loudness and satisfaction perceptions, suggesting sensitivity to relative changes rather than absolute background noise.

The preference for natural sounds (bird, water, wind, insect) and aversion to mechanical sounds (traffic, construction) drive overall soundscape preference, indicating a demand for restorative acoustic environments.
implementation_implications: Soundscape development should focus on inserting natural sounds and eliminating mechanical sounds in urban parks.
Better allocation of public spaces can help spread out people and reduce human-made sounds.
Noise masking with preferable sounds (e.g., water sounds) can modify built public environments to improve user experience.

Environmental monitoring should prioritize maximum noise levels and metrics related to spectral and temporal content of the acoustic environment, rather than solely relying on traditional LAeq monitoring.
Designs should aim for more quiet and pleasant acoustic environments to improve visitor satisfaction and encourage higher visit frequency.

tables.description: Summary of the questions in the self-administrated questionnaire survey, detailing parts, questions, number of questions, and scales used.

Measured acoustic metrics in the five locations at Sha Tin Park of Hong Kong, including time-equivalent, maximum, and statistical sound levels, as well as psychoacoustic metrics (total loudness, sharpness).

Subjects' soundscape perceptions (Pleasantness, Loudness, Sound variation, Satisfaction) in the five evaluated locations and grouped environments (Garden vs. Playground), including means, standard deviations, and Mann-Whitney U / Kruskal-Wallis test results with post-hoc comparisons.
key_stats: Mann-Whitney U test (G vs P) p<0.001 for Pleasantness, Loudness, Satisfaction; p=0.015 for Sound variation
Kruskal-Wallis test p<0.001 for Pleasantness, Loudness, Satisfaction; p=0.004 for Sound variation

tables.description: Spearman's rank correlation coefficients between the acoustic characteristics (Seq, LAmax, Nmax, LA10 - LA90) and the subjects' soundscape perceptions (Pleasantness, Loudness, Sound variation, Satisfaction).
Stepwise linear regression of subjects' satisfaction from other soundscape perceptions (Pleasantness, Loudness).

Results of the principal component analysis of the subjects' preferences for the 11 soundscape elements, showing factor loadings for three components: Natural sounds, Human sounds, and Mechanical sounds.
Stepwise linear regression of subjects' overall preference for a good soundscape from pleasantness perception, preference score of natural sounds, and visit frequency.
key_stats: beta for Preference score of Natural sounds = 0.25, p = 0.001

limitations: The spectral variation of sounds in similar acoustic environments might have been inadequate to detect effects on visitors' perceptions (pleasantness, satisfaction).
More soundscape evaluations in different urban parks with varied soundscape elements are needed to strengthen findings.
Inclusion of other acoustic metrics (temporal, spatial, annoyance, roughness, pleasantness) could provide a more comprehensive account of soundscape perceptions beyond loudness.
Difficulty in predicting maximum noise levels in outdoor environments due to random noise sources.
The study focused only on subjective responses; effects of noise on health quality (physiological, psychological responses) were not included.

More complicated designs are needed for integrated analyses of relationships between subjective responses of sound quality and other variables like health quality, age, education levels, gender, and nationality.
